DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.
Office hours this week move to Wednesday 3-5 pm in Lowry 118 because of the department colloquium.

DLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 TA recitation handout - Elasticity quick guide
DLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Recitation Handout - Week 6
Elasticity Quick Guide
Prepared by TA Marcus Delacroix-Byrne for the Friday recitation sections

Formula
Own-price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, where each percentage change is computed from the ORIGINAL value:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / Q1
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / P1
Keep the negative sign. A demand elasticity of -1.5 should be written as -1.5 so the grader can see you know demand slopes down.

Classification
- E below -1 (for example -1.5): elastic
- E between -1 and 0: inelastic
- E equal to -1: for this course, treat unit elastic as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same.

Practice example: the Quad coffee cart
The cart raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60 and daily sales fall from 500 to 400 cups.
% change in Q = -100 / 500 = -20%
% change in P = 0.60 / 3.00 = 20%
E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, so demand here is elastic (unit elastic counts as elastic).

Total revenue
Revenue before: $1,500 per day. Revenue after: $1,440 per day. Because the cart is on the elastic side, revenue moves in the opposite direction from price.

Exam tips
- On Midterm 2 either the original-value method or the midpoint method gets full credit, so use whichever is faster for you.
- A formula sheet will be stapled to the back of Midterm 2, so you do not need to memorize the formulas.
- Cross-price elasticity: take the absolute value, same as own-price, and report it to two decimals.
- If a question does not say which price is the starting price, use the lower price as the base.

Office hours for recitation questions: Fridays 1-2 pm, Econ Commons table 4.

DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

DLEC-CTX-I1.title: Rennick Library group study room policy
DLEC-CTX-I1.text:
Rennick Library - Group Study Room Policy (Fall Term)

Group study rooms on floors 2 and 3 of Rennick Library can be reserved by current students through the library booking portal. Each room holds between four and eight people and has a wall-mounted display and a whiteboard.

Booking rules
- Reservations open seven days in advance at 8:00 am.
- Each student may hold up to two hours of bookings per day and six hours per week.
- A room is released to the waitlist if nobody from the group checks in at the front desk within 15 minutes of the start time.
- Rooms 3B and 3C are quiet rooms: whiteboard work only, no calls or video meetings.

During exam weeks
- The daily limit drops to 90 minutes so more groups get a turn.
- Overnight booking between midnight and 7:00 am is available only on floor 2.

Care of rooms
- Wipe the whiteboard and take your rubbish with you when you leave.
- Food is not allowed; covered drinks are fine.
- Report broken displays or dried-out markers at the front desk or through the portal's "Report a problem" link.

Repeated no-shows (three in one term) suspend booking privileges for two weeks. Questions: ask at the Rennick front desk or contact the circulation team through the library website.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: simpler please
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).

NATIVELY: Start at floor(n/2) because everything past that index is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap, so there's nothing to fix. Sift-down only matters for nodes with children.

In the example, n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then continues down and swaps 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only sift a short distance. Summing each node's height over the whole tree stays linear in n.
items.answer:
Start at floor(n/2) because everything after that index is a leaf, and a leaf is already a valid heap on its own, so there's nothing to fix. Sift-down only does work on nodes that have children.

In the example, n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then keeps going and swaps 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n) and not O(n log n) because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only sift a short distance. Add up each node's height across the whole tree and the total stays linear in n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: are heaps on quiz 4? and is heapsort on it too?
items.answer: Heaps are on Quiz 4: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas, all in the 1-indexed layout. Heapsort isn't. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: accuracy vs precision?
conversation: PROFESSOR: One announcement, the career fair is Thursday in the student union, and the engineering firms are there from ten to two.
PROFESSOR: Bring printed copies of your resume, some recruiters still want paper.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value, while precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. You can be precise but not accurate, like a scale that always reads two pounds heavy, and accurate on average but not precise, like readings that scatter around the true value. In short, accuracy is about correctness, precision is about consistency.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: the handout says the coffee cart is unit elastic at -1.00 but I'm pretty sure she said elastic in lecture. which one is right, what should I write on the midterm, and why would they come out different?
items.answer:
Write **elastic**. The handout's own classification rule says that for this course, E equal to -1 is treated as elastic because the revenue logic is the same, and the coffee cart example lands at exactly -1.00, so it's labeled elastic there too.

They only look different because of wording. Unit elastic is the strict name for E = -1, while elastic is the broader bucket this course uses to cover E at or below -1. Same number, two labels, and the handout tells you which one the grader wants.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So remember, when demand is elastic and you raise the price, total revenue goes up, and that's exactly why the cart owner did it.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Okay, back to the coffee cart outside Benning Hall. Price goes from three dollars to three sixty.
PROFESSOR: Sales drop from five hundred cups a day to four hundred, and with our midpoint formula that's an elasticity of one point two two.
PROFESSOR: So demand is elastic over that range.
items.answer: The lecturer's claim is backwards. With elastic demand, a price increase **lowers** total revenue, not raises it. Check the numbers: before, $3.00 × 500 = $1,500 a day; after, $3.60 × 400 = $1,440 a day. Revenue fell by $60, which is exactly what the rule predicts for elastic demand. So the cart owner's price hike actually cost them money, and the slides say the same thing.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok so what does it solve to, and show me how you get there
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a **recurrence relation**. It's a compact way of saying how much work an algorithm does, written in terms of itself on a smaller input.

Read it piece by piece. T(n) is the total time to sort n items. The **2T(n/2)** means the algorithm splits the problem into 2 subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the extra work done at this level, outside the recursive calls, and for merge sort that's the merging step, which touches all n elements.

So merge sort sorts two halves of size n/2, then spends linear time merging them back together. You solve the recurrence with the master theorem or a recursion tree, and here it comes out to Theta(n log n).
USER (typed to Natively): why n/2?

NATIVELY: The **n/2** is the size of each subproblem. Merge sort splits the array into two halves, so if the whole thing has n elements, each half has n/2. That's why the recursive part is 2T(n/2): two calls, each on half the input.

The n inside Theta(n) is different. That's the merge step, which touches all n elements at this level, not half of them. So the two numbers play different roles: n/2 is how big each piece is, n is how much work you do putting them back together.
items.answer:
Solving it means finding the closed form for T(n), and for this recurrence it comes out to **Theta(n log n)**. Here's how you get there.

Use the recursion tree. At the top level you do Theta(n) work. That splits into 2 subproblems of size n/2, and each of those does Theta(n/2) work, so the level total is 2 times n/2, which is n again. Next level: 4 subproblems of size n/4, each doing n/4, so 4 times n/4, still n. Every level costs n.

The number of levels is how many times you can halve n before hitting size 1, which is log n. So total work is n per level times log n levels, giving Theta(n log n).

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Which means we're basically 97 percent sure the drug works.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.

NATIVELY: That's a common misreading, actually. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, there'd be a 3% chance of seeing data at least as extreme as what you got. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. To get the chance the null is true, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior.
items.answer: No, that's the same flip in the other direction. The p-value says nothing about the chance the drug works, so you can't just subtract it from 100. A p-value of 0.03 means that if there were truly no effect, you'd see data this extreme about 3 percent of the time. The probability the drug actually works is a different quantity, and getting it needs a prior plus the data, not 1 minus the p-value.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: what did he say about the second law earlier, and how does it connect to this?
items.answer: I can't pull up what he said earlier, since I don't have the lecture transcript in front of me. But the second law itself is worth restating: entropy in an isolated system never decreases, so heat flows from hot to cold on its own and never the reverse without work being put in. That's why any real engine has to dump some heat to a cold reservoir, and it's the reason no cycle can be perfectly efficient. If you tell me which part of today's material he was connecting it to, I can tie it in directly.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain simpler: what's the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the curve? she lost me
items.answer:
A movement along the curve happens when only the **price** changes. Price goes down, you slide to a point further right on the same curve, quantity demanded rises. The curve itself doesn't move.

A shift happens when something other than price changes, like income, tastes, or the price of a related good. Then the whole curve moves to a new position, so at every price people want a different quantity.

Quick test: if the only thing that changed is the good's own price, it's a movement. If anything else changed, it's a shift.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.
items.answer: The Peace of Westphalia is actually two treaties signed in 1648, in Münster and Osnabrück, that ended both the Thirty Years' War in the Empire and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. Its reputation as the birth of the sovereign state system comes mainly from the idea of **cuius regio, eius religio** extended further, letting each territory's ruler settle religion, and from the way it treated the Empire's princes as having real standing of their own. Historians do push back on the "Westphalian sovereignty" story, since the treaties still left the Emperor and the Empire's institutions in place, and sovereignty as a formal doctrine came later, with Bodin and then the nineteenth century. So it's a useful marker, but more of a milestone than a clean break.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.
items.answer: The key idea is that confessing is a **dominant strategy**: it gives each prisoner a better outcome regardless of what the other does. If the other stays quiet, confessing means a lighter sentence. If the other confesses, confessing still beats staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they had both stayed quiet. That gap between individual rationality and collective benefit is the dilemma.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: teach me Bayes' theorem properly. start from what conditional probability actually means, derive the formula, then walk me through a disease screening example with real numbers, and finish with the mistake people make most often with it.
items.answer:
Conditional probability is just probability once you know something. P(A|B) means the chance of A, given that B is true, so we shrink our world down to only the cases where B happened and ask what fraction of those are also A. That gives the definition: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Bayes' theorem falls out of that almost immediately. Since P(A and B) equals P(B|A) times P(A), we can substitute and get P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B). The intuition: your prior belief P(A) gets reweighted by how much more likely the evidence B is under A than overall.

For the screening example, take a disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people, so P(D) = 0.001. The test catches 99% of sick people, so P(+|D) = 0.99, and it falsely flags 5% of healthy people, so P(+|no D) = 0.05. The total positive rate is P(+) = 0.99 × 0.001 + 0.05 × 0.999 = 0.00099 + 0.04995 = 0.05094. So P(D|+) = 0.00099 / 0.05094, which is about **1.9%**. A positive result on a 99%-sensitive test still means under a 2% chance of actually being sick, because the disease is rare and the false positives swamp the true ones.

The mistake people make most often is the base rate fallacy: they read P(+|D) as if it were P(D|+), ignoring how rare the condition is. The two are completely different numbers, and confusing them is exactly what flips that 1.9% into a false 99%.

items.question: So what happens if I increase the pressure on nitrogen plus three hydrogen going to two ammonia? Somebody?
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.

NATIVELY: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium reacts to a disturbance by shifting in whichever direction partially counteracts it. So if you add more of a reactant, the equilibrium moves toward the products to use some of it up. If you increase pressure by shrinking the volume, it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. And if you raise the temperature, it shifts in the endothermic direction, the one that absorbs the added heat. The key idea is that the shift is only partial, it eases the disturbance without fully canceling it.
items.answer: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the ammonia, because that's the side with fewer gas molecules. On the left you have four molecules of gas, one nitrogen plus three hydrogen, and on the right just two ammonia, so the system relieves the squeeze by favoring the side that takes up less space. That's exactly why the Haber process runs at high pressure.

items.question: what did she mean by 'the corridor is really just a floor'?
conversation: PROFESSOR: The Fed doesn't really set 'the interest rate.' It sets a target range for the federal funds rate.
PROFESSOR: Back when reserves were scarce, it hit that target with open market operations, buying and selling securities pretty much every day.
PROFESSOR: Now we're in an ample reserves regime, so the main tool is the interest rate on reserve balances, and honestly the corridor is really just a floor.
items.answer: She means the "corridor" isn't a symmetric band anymore. In an ample reserves regime, the Fed's main tool is the interest rate on reserve balances, which acts as a floor under short term rates, so the effective ceiling comes from other facilities rather than a matching top. So the corridor is really just a floor.

items.question: So, can anyone tell me why the sky is blue but sunsets are red? Anybody? Think about wavelength, and think about how much air the light has to go through.
items.answer:
Sunlight contains all colors, but it has to pass through the atmosphere to reach us. Air molecules scatter short wavelengths, the blues and violets, far more than long ones, so blue light gets bounced around the sky in every direction and that's what we see overhead. At sunset the light travels through much more air because it comes in at a low angle, and by then the blue has been scattered away, leaving the longer reds and oranges to reach our eyes directly.

**Rayleigh scattering** is the name for that wavelength dependence, and the amount of atmosphere the light crosses is the other half of the answer.

items.question: And that's why the firm's short-run supply curve is just its marginal cost curve, but only the part above the minimum of AVC.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Remember from Tuesday, marginal cost is what it costs to make one more unit, and the MC curve crosses average variable cost at its minimum.
PROFESSOR: And the shutdown rule: in the short run a firm keeps producing as long as price covers average variable cost, not average total cost. Fixed costs are sunk either way.
PROFESSOR: Okay, let's draw the firm's cost curves again.
items.answer: The short-run supply curve is the MC curve above the minimum of AVC because of the shutdown rule. A firm produces where price equals marginal cost, so every price above that minimum maps to a quantity on the MC curve. Below the minimum of AVC, price doesn't even cover variable cost, so the firm shuts down and supplies zero. That's why the supply curve starts at the bottom of AVC, not at the bottom of ATC.

items.question: Now repeat it forever.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.

NATIVELY: The key idea is that confessing is a **dominant strategy**: it gives each prisoner a better outcome regardless of what the other does. If the other stays quiet, confessing means a lighter sentence. If the other confesses, confessing still beats staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they had both stayed quiet. That gap between individual rationality and collective benefit is the dilemma.
items.answer: That's the setup for an iterated prisoner's dilemma. When the game repeats indefinitely, the calculation changes: each player now has to weigh today's payoff against how the other will respond tomorrow. Cooperation can become rational, because defecting today invites retaliation in future rounds. The classic result is that a tit-for-tat strategy, cooperating first and then mirroring the other player's last move, tends to do well, since it rewards cooperation and punishes defection without escalating. So repetition is what makes sustained cooperation possible where a one-shot game drives both to confess.

items.question: explain gradient descent using an example from my own work experience so it actually sticks
items.answer:
Gradient descent is just walking downhill on a loss surface: you compute the slope, take a small step opposite it, and repeat. The step size is the learning rate. Too big and you overshoot, too small and you crawl.
